title: Residual-Based Time Discretization on Nonlinear Approximation Manifolds: Analysis and Gaussian Applications
abstract: We study time-discrete parametric approximations of evolution equations in Hilbert spaces based on residual minimization. The solution is represented by a parametrized ansatz belonging to a low-dimensional nonlinear manifold, and time stepping is performed by minimizing suitably defined residuals at each step. Two natural residual formulations are considered: discretization followed by parametrization of the evolution equation, and discretization of the Dirac--Frenkel variational principle governing the parameter dynamics. A unified error analysis is developed for both approaches within the family of $ζ$-methods. The resulting bounds separate the effects of time discretization from those of residual minimization and yield first- and second-order convergence under Lipschitz, one-sided Lipschitz, and dissipativity assumptions. For the variational formulation, additional stability conditions involving the conditioning of the parametrization map arise naturally. The framework is applied to Gaussian approximation manifolds, for which residual norms and gradients admit explicit closed-form expressions when polynomial operators are involved. This enables efficient implementation without spatial discretization. Numerical experiments for time-dependent Schrödinger equations illustrate the theoretical convergence rates and the influence of residual accuracy on conservation properties.
summary: This paper presents a unified theoretical framework for analyzing time-stepping methods that approximate solutions to evolution equations by minimizing residuals on low-dimensional nonlinear manifolds. It rigorously separates and bounds the errors arising from both the time discretization scheme ($\zeta$-methods) and the residual minimization process itself. This is highly valuable for developing stable and accurate numerical solvers for quantum dynamics simulations.
main_problem: Developing a unified error analysis for time-discrete parametric approximations of evolution equations posed in Hilbert spaces.
main_result: The global approximation error can be decomposed into separate residual and time discretization components, achieving convergence rates up to second order under various stability assumptions.
method: The core method involves iteratively minimizing a residual norm (derived from either discretizing the equation then parameterizing, or parametrizing then discretizing the variational principle) at each time step.
model_or_system: The theory is applied to general evolution equations in Hilbert spaces, specifically illustrated using time-dependent Schrödinger and Fokker–Planck equations. The solution is approximated by a parametrized ansatz on a low-dimensional nonlinear manifold.
key_observables: Global approximation error, residual norms, and gradients of the cost function $F_k(	heta) = \|r_k(	heta, \cdot)\|^2_H$.
important_parameters: Time step size ($h$), total time ($T$), and the structure/conditioning of the parametrization map.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on Lipschitz, one-sided Lipschitz, or dissipativity assumptions for convergence guarantees; stability conditions involving parametrization map conditioning arise naturally in certain formulations.
figures_summary: Figure 10 shows the evolution of a single Gaussian wave packet under different regimes of the Fokker–Planck equation. Figure 11 illustrates the squared $L_2$-norm difference between exact and numerical solutions for this example, showing convergence with step size.
paper_structure: The paper introduces an abstract framework (Section 2), derives explicit residual formulations based on two paradigms (Section 3), develops a unified error analysis for $\zeta$-methods (Section 4), and details closed-form formulas for Gaussian manifolds (Section 5).
why_interesting: This work provides rigorous mathematical tools to analyze the convergence of complex numerical schemes used in quantum dynamics, particularly those involving variational parameterizations common in AMO physics.
